record_reviews.summary: Blyth’s extensive notes range from a general theory of domesticated variation to concrete cases: abnormal forms propagated by human selection versus normal geographic races; fowl ancestry and wild Gallus voices; variable ruffs, birds, mammals, shells and plant markings; reindeer, camels and humped cattle; and the rapid establishment of an introduced Achatina snail in Lower Bengal. The notes also contain Blyth’s challenges to Lyell’s zoological premises, reports of his own observations, and questions for Darwin. The final paragraph says he has begun reading Lyell and will write a corrective letter, so its zoology and its prospective Lyell critique should not be collapsed into one dated event. Body sections: P1–P5 distinguish casual monstrosities selected by people from geographically normal races, classify domestic animals by known/probable/unknown origin, and discuss fowl/pigeon ancestry. P6–P10 give variability in wild birds, ruffs, size, bilateral markings and plant forms. P11–P16 address reindeer, camels, cattle and sheep, with P13 explicitly quoting Blyth’s earlier writing. P17–P22 extend variation examples across bear, birds, shells, mammals and plants. P23–P27 compare reindeer, camels and Bos indicus, including the claim that the hump is muscular and fetal rather than a fat-tailed-sheep abnormality. P28–P30 report Asian naming, orangutan/hippopotamus taxonomy, and the introduction of Achatina perdix from Mauritius by a single pair. P31 says Lyell’s premises contain errors and announces a future rectification.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The displayed heading is [30 September or 7 October 1855], with XML bounds 1855-09-30 through 1855-10-07 and a mutually exclusive date alternative. The editorial footnote derives the range from “Sunday morning” and Blyth’s 8 October statement that the notes went in that day’s post; CD’s “December 1855” receipt annotation is a separate layer. This is a memorandum originally enclosed with the 8 October letter DCP-LETT-1760, not an independently dated conventional letter; composition, enclosure, dispatch, and CD receipt remain distinct.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Blyth voice throughout the notes, including quoted passages he identifies as his earlier article. P25 contains a quoted/previous Blyth passage on reindeer domestication; P31 reports his reading and intended critique of Lyell. CD annotations, footnotes, bibliography, and the enclosure history are editorial or later layers and are not silently promoted to body voice.

record_reviews.summary: Blyth explains that he recalled accompanying memoranda after receiving Thomas Hutton’s replies to questions he had sent for Darwin, then transcribes Hutton on rabbits, canaries, geese, hill cats and pigeons. Blyth adds his own qualifications about European station introductions, identifies possible Himalayan cats, cites Chinese cormorants and Middle Asian silkworms, and promises further photographs and the jungle-fowl skeleton. Quotation marks and Blyth’s intervening remarks preserve Hutton’s voice separately. Body sections: No Darwin prompt is preserved here. The opening proves Blyth was answering queries sent to Hutton for Darwin and that accompanying memoranda were separate, but does not identify or reproduce those queries.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML bounds 22–23 August 1855; the heading is a bounded range and exact order needs review. P1 says the memoranda had been despatched and recalled, while P15/P16 place the signed letter and postscript on 23 August. Those logistics do not date Hutton’s underlying letter exactly.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Blyth’s letter voice surrounds explicitly quoted Hutton material in P2–P6. Hutton is an evidentiary third-party observer; Blyth’s questions, corrections and promises remain Blyth.

record_reviews.source_kind: preserved HTML letter or memorandum with complete scholarly apparatus
record_reviews.summary: Blyth first corrects Hutton’s identification of Felis himalayanus, arguing from a remembered specimen and museum comparison that it is F. viverrinus, then treats Bali banteng, a possible Burmese cattle species, domesticated gayals, rabbit albinos, jackal–pariah hybrids and the species/race problem. He gives a substantive Columba intermedia/livia discussion and compares wolves, squirrels and mustelids, insisting that behavior and voice can distinguish species despite close form. Body sections: The letter contains answers to Darwin’s questions (P7 begins “You ask”), but the underlying Darwin question letter is not preserved in the packet. Later Blyth correspondence cannot substitute for it.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 7 September 1855 is the XML single-day bound, with a bracketed display date. P7 is explicitly dated “Septr—7” within the body; composition is secure to that day, while posting and Darwin’s receipt are unrecorded.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Blyth body voice; Hutton, Jardine, Schlegel, Temminck, Gould and other authorities are reported or challenged. No quoted correspondent is silently treated as sender.

record_reviews.summary: Blyth forwards Robert Tickell’s Tenasserim observations on otters, rabbits and geese, then adds his own extended discussion of wolves, reason and instinct, animal learning, hybrid fertility, human variation and domestication. The source shifts between Tickell’s quoted report, Blyth’s argument and references to Prichard and other authorities; the ending turns to seed dispersal, cultivated plants and promised follow-up. Body sections: This is a continuation of Blyth’s domestic-animal exchange, but no uniquely preserved Darwin prompt is included. Shared subjects with 1670, 1735 or 1761 are continuation evidence only and cannot establish a pair.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The heading gives [22 September 1855], and XML bounds are 1855-09-22 to 1855-09-22 with bracketed date qualification. The composition/date remains editorially conjectured; no dispatch or Darwin receipt is shown.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Blyth is author of the framing letter and argument. Tickell’s material is explicitly forwarded/quoted third-party evidence; Prichard and other named writers are cited voices.
